# Ischemic hepatitis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the liver > Ischemic hepatitis*

[Original Article Link](/library/Hs0Kwh)

---

## Summary

<u>Ischemic</u> <u>hepatitis</u> is acute, diffuse hepatocellular injury due to hepatic <u>hypoperfusion</u>. The most common causes are cardiopulmonary failure and <u>sepsis</u>. Clinical features are mostly related to the underlying cause, and symptoms related to <u>liver</u> injury (e.g., abdominal <u>pain</u>, <u>nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>, and <u>anorexia</u>) may be absent. Diagnosis is based on the clinical context and characteristic laboratory findings, such as a transient severe elevation of serum <u>aminotransferases</u> and increased levels of <u>LDH</u> and <u>bilirubin</u>. Management focuses on prompt identification, treatment of the underlying cause, and <u>hemodynamic support</u>. With appropriate intervention, hepatic injury is often reversible.

---

## Etiology

* Impaired hepatic <u>perfusion</u>: <u>heart failure</u>, severe <u>hypotension</u>, <u>cardiogenic shock</u>, <u>hypovolemic shock</u>, <u>thromboembolism</u>, <u>cardiac tamponade</u>

* <u>Hypoxemia</u>: <u>respiratory failure</u>

* Increased metabolic demand: <u>septic shock</u>, extensive <u>burns</u>, <u>surgery</u>





> [!WARNING]
> Referring to <u>ischemic</u> <u>hepatitis</u> as “shock liver” is not recommended, as <u>hypoxic</u> <u>liver</u> injury can occur without <u>shock</u>. [[4]](/library/xEdEB70)

---

## Clinical features

* Symptoms related to <u>liver</u> injury may be absent.

* Fatigue, <u>weakness</u>, <u>altered mental status</u> (<u>AMS</u>)

* <u>Hypotension</u>, <u>tachycardia</u>

* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>, <u>anorexia</u>, <u>right upper quadrant</u> tenderness, <u>hepatomegaly</u>

* Clinical features of associated complications (e.g., <u>hepatopulmonary syndrome</u>, <u>hyperglycemia</u>, <u>hypoglycemia</u>, and/or <u>hyperammonemia</u>)

---

## Diagnosis

### General principles [[5]](/library/Eud8G70)




* Suspect <u>ischemic</u> <u>hepatitis</u> in patients with both:

* <u>Hemodynamic instability</u> and/or <u>respiratory failure</u>

* Transient <u>severe transaminitis</u> and elevated <u>LDH</u> levels

* Exclude alternative <u>causes of elevated transaminases</u> (e.g., <u>acetaminophen toxicity</u>, <u>acute viral hepatitis</u>).

* Imaging and <u>biopsy</u> are not required for diagnosis.





### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[5]](/library/Eud8G70)




* <u>Liver function</u> tests

* <u>Severe transaminitis</u> [[4]](/library/xEdEB70)

* Typically <u>AST</u> > <u>ALT</u>; levels often > 1000 U/L  [[6]](/library/2vdTz70)

* Serum levels peak 1–3 days after <u>ischemic</u> injury and typically normalize within 7–14 days. [[6]](/library/2vdTz70)

* ↑ <u>Bilirubin</u>

* ↑ <u>LDH</u>

* <u>ALT</u>:<u>LDH</u> <u>ratio</u> < 1.5  [[7]](/library/ZEdZ870)

* Normal <u>alkaline phosphatase</u>

* <u>Renal function tests</u>: Serum <u>creatinine</u> and <u>BUN</u> may be elevated.  [[8]](/library/NEd-D70)

* <u>Coagulation studies</u>: <u>INR</u> and <u>prothrombin time</u> may be prolonged.

* Tests to exclude other causes of <u>acute liver injury</u>, e.g.:

* <u>Acetaminophen levels</u> (see “<u>Acetaminophen overdose</u>.”)

* <u>Acute viral hepatitis panel</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>AST</u> > 400 U/L should raise concern for <u>ischemic</u> <u>hepatitis</u> or <u>drug-induced liver injury</u>. [[9]](/library/QtcuWV0)




### Imaging studies [[5]](/library/Eud8G70)




* Abdominal <u>ultrasound</u> with Doppler: to evaluate vasculature (e.g., dilated <u>hepatic veins</u>, abnormal flow in hepatic <u>artery</u> or <u>portal vein</u>)

* <u>Echocardiogram</u>: may show evidence of cardiac dysfunction

---

## Pathology

* Diffuse hepatic injury

* <u>Centrilobular necrosis</u> (zone 3 of the <u>hepatic acinus</u>) with very few inflammatory cells

---

## Differential diagnoses

* <u>Drug-induced liver injury</u> (due to, e.g., <u>acetaminophen</u>;  or herbal supplement <u>poisoning</u>)

* <u>Acute viral hepatitis</u>

* <u>Hepatic infarction</u>

* See “<u>Common causes of severe elevation of transaminases</u>.”




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Management

There is no specific treatment for <u>ischemic</u> <u>hepatitis</u>. [[5]](/library/Eud8G70)




* Provide <u>management of acute liver failure</u> if present.

* Treat the underlying cause.

* Provide <u>hemodynamic support</u> and optimize <u>cardiac output</u> (e.g., with <u>diuretics</u> in <u>hypervolemia</u>).

* Consult hepatology for patients who do not improve with supportive management.

* Monitor for evidence of end-organ <u>hypoperfusion</u> with, e.g.:

* Serial <u>BMPs</u> for <u>renal failure</u>

* <u>Confusion assessment method</u> for <u>AMS</u>
